scenes.heading: Organic reactions
scenes.sub: Turning one functional group into another
scenes.say: Organic reactions turn one functional group into another, like making esters for flavours. Let's meet the main reaction types and how to judge them.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Players join, get subbed, or two teams merge and one person leaves
scenes.breaks: players move freely, but each reaction needs specific reagents and conditions, like a catalyst or UV light.
scenes.say: Think of a footy team. Addition is two players joining with nobody leaving. Substitution is one player subbed off for another. Condensation is two teams merging, but the water boy has to leave. That water boy is a water molecule.

scenes.heading: Addition to alkenes
points: C=C opens and adds an atom to each C
scenes.say: Alkenes do addition: the double bond opens up and grabs a new atom on each carbon. Add hydrogen with a nickel catalyst, or steam with a phosphoric acid catalyst to make an alcohol. Bromine water going colourless is the test for a C double bond C.
scenes.caption: Alkenes do addition: the double bond opens up and grabs a new atom on each carbon. Add H₂ with a nickel catalyst, or steam with an H₃PO₄ catalyst to make an alcohol. Bromine water going colourless is the test for a C=C.

scenes.heading: Substitution and condensation
points: Alkane + Cl₂ in UV light → haloalkane
scenes.say: Substitution swaps one group for another. In UV light, an alkane swaps a hydrogen for a halogen, and a haloalkane can become an alcohol or an amine. Condensation joins an acid to an alcohol or an amine, releasing water, to make an ester or an amide.

scenes.heading: Oxidising alcohols
scenes.say: Acidified dichromate pulls an H off the carbon holding the O H. Primary alcohols go all the way to carboxylic acids, secondary stop at ketones, and tertiary just sit there, because that carbon has no hydrogen to lose. Dichromate turns from orange to green.
scenes.caption: Acidified dichromate pulls an H off the carbon holding the –OH. Primary alcohols go all the way to carboxylic acids, secondary stop at ketones, and tertiary just sit there, because that carbon has no H to lose. Dichromate turns from orange to green.

scenes.heading: Atom economy vs yield
scenes.say: Atom economy is on paper: the molar mass of the product you want, divided by all the reactants, times a hundred. Percentage yield is in the lab: actual over theoretical. A reaction can have perfect atom economy and still a low yield.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: 12.0 g of ethanoic acid (M = 60.0) and excess ethanol give 14.1 g of ethyl ethanoate (M = 88.0). Find the % yield.
scenes.say: Twelve grams of ethanoic acid is zero point two zero zero moles, so in theory you get zero point two zero zero moles of ester: seventeen point six grams. You collected fourteen point one, so the yield is eighty point one percent.
scenes.caption: 12.0 g of ethanoic acid is 0.200 mol, so in theory you get 0.200 mol of ester: 17.6 g. You collected 14.1 g, so the yield is 80.1%.

scenes.say: Quick recap. Addition keeps everything. Substitution swaps, and condensation loses water. Primary alcohols go all the way, secondary stop at ketones, and tertiary don't react. Now try the practice questions!
